title: AI Platform Engineering: Patrick Debois

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building shared AI platform infrastructure—model access, registries, observability, eval monitoring, caching, guardrails, and feedback services—that other engineering teams consume. The talk targets developer platforms as the vertical and draws general-purpose organizational lessons from DevOps adoption patterns applicable across domains. The talk spans development enablement, testing methodology, model deployment and migration, production monitoring, and governance controls. The speaker assumes familiarity with DevOps, platform engineering, and genAI concepts, targeting practicing engineers and engineering leaders. Recorded live conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair with audience Q&A. Multiple direct transcript excerpts ground the classification across platform components, team organization, testing, and governance.

summary: Patrick Debois establishes his credentials as the coiner of DevOps and organizer of the first DevOpsDays in 2009, using this background to argue that AI platform engineering follows the same pilot-to-scale adoption pattern seen with Cloud, DevOps, and SecOps. He compares the broad label 'AI engineer' to 'DevOps' as a searchable term that helps practitioners find each other. He describes organizational friction between data science and engineering teams during genAI adoption and how capability eventually moves into a shared platform team, using Team Topologies as the organizing framework. He catalogs AI platform components: model access/proxies, vector databases, data connectors, model registries, prompt observability, eval-based production monitoring, caching, and feedback-as-a-service. Enablement is emphasized as equally critical—prototyping tools, local dev environments, secure data experimentation, and learning frameworks drive adoption. He details developer experience pains: engineers struggle with model selection, test data access, and framework instability; model migration is costly, with eight model changes over two years requiring manual prompt rework. Testing genAI requires a layered approach from exact matching through semantic distance, LLM-as-judge, and human feedback. He notes the productivity paradox of AI coding tools: generation speeds up but review times increase and PR sizes grow, citing the 'Ironies of GenAI Automation' paper. He draws a parallel to DevOps evolution—automation led to CI/CD, monitoring, observability, and chaos engineering. Governance covers personal awareness, data leakage, model licensing, EU risk-level assessment, prompt injection defenses, guardrails, and PII monitoring. He introduces the 'unfixed model' as an alternative to Team Topologies, featuring an experience crew for consistent AI UX. He concludes that cross-collaboration among CloudOps, SecOps, DevEx, Data Platform, and AI Platform teams is the pattern for organizations scaling to 10+ teams. In a brief Q&A, an audience member asks about the guardrails-as-a-service paradigm—whether guardrails should sit in front of all models with model cards specifying which are applied, or whether product teams consume guardrails under their own remit. Debois answers that central governance teams put generic rules in place while individual teams layer their own use-case-specific rules on top, combining self-service with a centralized component so teams do not duplicate rules.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Background and DevOps Parallel
sections.summary: Debois establishes his DevOps credentials and explains how 15 years of observing technology transformations informs his view of AI platform engineering. He describes the pilot-to-scale adoption pattern and compares the 'AI engineer' label to 'DevOps' as a searchable term for finding practitioners.

sections.title: Organizational Friction and Team Topologies
sections.summary: Describes friction between data science and engineering teams during genAI adoption, how engineers absorbed into data science teams, and how capability eventually moved to a platform team. Introduces Team Topologies as the framework for organizing platform teams that abstract complexity for feature teams.

sections.title: AI Platform Components
sections.summary: Catalogs shared AI platform services: model access and proxies, vector databases, data connectors, model version control/registries, cloud-agnostic access control, prompt observability, eval-based production monitoring, caching, and feedback-as-a-service with inline editing.

sections.title: Enablement and Local Dev
sections.summary: Addresses how platform teams guide customers to use infrastructure through prototyping tools, secure data experimentation, including product owners, and learning frameworks. Local dev environments with quality models on laptops help engineers iterate faster, though pitfalls include unclear use cases, over-focus on fine-tuning, premature cost optimization, and engineers not knowing how to handle end-user feedback.

sections.title: Developer Experience Pains and Model Migration
sections.summary: Details genAI developer pains: model selection uncertainty, test data access difficulty, framework instability causing teams to work at lower layers. Model migration over two years involved eight different LLMs, each requiring manual prompt rework, highlighting the need for evals before refactoring.

sections.title: Testing GenAI Applications
sections.summary: Explains the layered testing approach for genAI: exact testing with regex, sentiment checks using helper models, semantic distance for question-answer relevance, LLM-as-judge for evaluating LLM output, and human feedback as the final layer.

sections.title: AI Coding Tools Productivity Paradox
sections.summary: Discusses how AI coding tools like Copilot increase code generation speed but also increase review times and PR sizes. Cites the 'Ironies of GenAI Automation' paper, warning that the shift from producer to reviewer risks losing situational awareness, with a anecdote about higher weekend acceptance rates due to reduced developer attention.

sections.title: DevOps Evolution Parallel and Governance
sections.summary: Draws parallel to DevOps evolution from automation through CI/CD, monitoring, design for failure, observability, and chaos engineering. Covers governance: personal awareness programs, data leakage risks, opt-out from training, model license and origin scrutiny, EU risk-level assessment, prompt injection defenses, guardrails, and PII monitoring.

sections.title: Platform Team Collaboration and Unfixed Model
sections.summary: Introduces the unfixed model as an alternative to Team Topologies, featuring an experience crew for consistent AI UX. Recommends cross-collaboration among CloudOps, SecOps, DevEx, Data Platform, and AI Platform teams for organizations scaling to 10+ teams, cautioning against premature optimization for small companies.

sections.title: Q&A: Guardrails as a Service
sections.summary: An audience member asks about the guardrails-as-a-service paradigm—whether guardrails should be placed in front of all models with model cards specifying which are applied, or whether product teams should consume guardrails under their own remit. Debois answers that central governance teams put generic rules in place while individual teams layer their own use-case-specific rules on top, combining self-service with a centralized component so teams do not duplicate rules.

limitations: Guardrails and prompt injection remain unsolved problems with overwhelming log volumes
Framework instability causes teams to abandon frameworks and work at lower abstraction layers
Engineers often don't know how to handle end-user feedback because product owners hold domain knowledge
quantitativeClaims: One prompt typically leads to 5-6 iterations/questions in production
Eight different LLM models were used over two years
AI-generated PRs were larger and review times increased after introducing Copilot
Weekend Copilot suggestion acceptance rates were higher because developers were less attentive
